title: Transmitting algebras through quantum channels
abstract: We develop a theory of exact transmission of finite-dimensional $C^*$-algebras through quantum channels. These algebras describe hybrid classical-quantum information, allowing the dimension of the quantum system to depend on the classical message. Allowing arbitrary encodings and decodings yields a transmission set of algebra types, ordered by embedding, that unifies zero-error information theory with operator-algebraic error correction. We ask if this set admits a dominating algebra into which every transmittable algebra embeds. Our central finding is that domination can fail even in small dimensions. In its absence, several incomparable maximal algebras can describe different optimal uses of the same channel, forcing the user to select one depending on the operational task and the type of information to be preserved. We introduce hybrid capacities that reconstruct the only possible dominating algebra type and present a complete finite characterization of domination using minimal forbidden algebra types. We identify dominating algebras for channels whose operator systems are graph-isomorphic to $*$-algebras, including highly divisible channels, and for channels with zero one-shot zero-error quantum capacity. Under tensor products, we prove that joint coding can produce new algebra types, giving an algebraic analogue of superadditivity from Shannon theory. Domination can fail for the joint use of two channels, even when both channels separately admit dominating algebras. Finally, we construct a channel whose $n$-fold tensor powers have doubly exponentially many maximal algebra types, attaining the largest possible growth scaling for finite-dimensional channels. Consequently, new transmittable algebra types appear at arbitrarily large block-lengths for this channel, so its full transmission structure cannot be generated from any finite collection of bounded-block-length codes.
summary: This work develops a rigorous theory for determining which complex information structures (C*-algebras) can be perfectly transmitted through a quantum channel. The central finding is that a single 'optimal' structure may not exist, forcing users to select different optimal strategies based on the specific task. This advances the understanding of quantum channel capacity by introducing algebraic invariants and characterizing when such universal structures fail to exist.
main_problem: The paper develops a theory to characterize the exact transmission of finite-dimensional C*-algebras through arbitrary quantum channels.
main_result: The existence of a unique 'dominating' algebra that encompasses all optimal transmission strategies is not guaranteed, and the failure of domination implies complex, task-dependent choices for the user.
method: The authors use algebraic methods involving embedding preorders on the set of transmittable algebras and introduce 'hybrid capacities' to characterize the structure.
model_or_system: The system involves quantum channels $\Phi: L(H) 	o L(K)$ acting on finite-dimensional C*-algebras, which model hybrid classical-quantum information.
key_observables: Transmittable algebras $T(\Phi)$, hybrid capacities, and the growth rate of maximal algebra types under tensor products.
important_parameters: The dimension of the algebras ($d_k$), the block-length of the code, and the structure of the quantum channel $\Phi$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the algebraic structure of the channel and the definition of transmittability via encoding/decoding channels.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the Hasse diagrams showing when a dominating algebra exists for specific channels, and classification diagrams relating channel structures to the existence of capacity algebras.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the mathematical framework for transmittable algebras, investigates the existence and properties of a dominating algebra, derives structural theorems for domination, and concludes with examples showing the failure of domination and superadditivity analogues.
why_interesting: It provides a deep algebraic framework for understanding information capacity limits, which is fundamental to quantum communication theory and quantum error correction.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Hasse diagrams of two possible transmission sets, with nonzero algebras identified up to ∗- isomorphism. An upward path from A to B means A ≤B; edges show only cover relations. Boxes mark maximal elements. In (a), the boxed algebra dominates every transmittable algebra. In (b), the two boxed algebras have no common upper bound in the transmission set.

Figure 2: Classes of channels admitting a capacity algebra and a dominating transmittable algebra. The two structural sufficient classes from Section 4.2 and 4.3 overlap, and neither contains the other; their union is strictly smaller than the class admitting a dominating algebra. The bottom line records further sufficient classes without depicting their intersections with the algebraic class.
